source: Dung (1995) On the acceptability of arguments and its fundamental role in nonmonotonic reasoning, logic programming and n-person games
finding: Founding paper. An argumentation framework is a set of arguments and one attack relation. Acceptability is decided only from the graph. Grounded, preferred and stable semantics are defined. Many nonmonotonic logics are shown to be special cases.
numbers: Theory paper, no experiments. Not opened this session (paywalled); definitions checked via the Modgil and Prakken tutorial (a02).
limits: Says nothing about argument content, so a separate step must build the graph and decide attacks.
agent_relevance: S7: candidates are nodes and 'fails the test the other passes' is an attack edge; the graph is the whole formal object.

source: Modgil and Prakken (2013) The ASPIC+ framework for structured argumentation: a tutorial
finding: Restates Dung. A set S is admissible if conflict free and every member is defended against all attackers. Complete, grounded (minimal complete), preferred (maximal complete) and stable extensions follow. A claim is sceptically justified if in all extensions, credulously if in at least one.
numbers: Definition 3.1 in the tutorial. The grounded extension is unique; preferred may be several; stable may not exist.
quote: S is the grounded extension iff it is the set inclusion minimal complete extension
limits: Abstract level only; ASPIC+ adds structure on top.
agent_relevance: Grounded semantics gives one answer in code with no ties; preferred gives several. For S7 grounded or sceptical acceptance is the safe default.

source: Modgil and Prakken (2013) ASPIC+ tutorial: structure and attack types
finding: ASPIC+ builds arguments from strict rules (premises guarantee conclusion) and defeasible rules (only a presumption). An argument can be attacked on an uncertain premise, on a defeasible inference step, or on the conclusion of a defeasible step. Conflicts are settled by explicit preferences.
numbers: Three attack types: undermining, undercutting, rebutting. Preferences turn attacks into defeats.
limits: Needs a logical language and rule sets; hard to apply to free text.
agent_relevance: Maps to code-run checks: a failing test is a rebuttal, a broken assumption is an undermine, a flawed step is an undercut.

source: Modgil and Prakken (2013) ASPIC+ tutorial: rationality postulates (Caminada and Amgoud 2007)
finding: Four postulates every complete extension should meet: sub-argument closure, closure under strict rules, direct consistency, indirect consistency. ASPIC+ satisfies all four only under conditions (closure under transposition or contraposition, reasonable preference ordering). Violations are shown with examples.
numbers: Section 4.2. A naive instantiation can accept two contradictory conclusions.
limits: Conditions are about logic-based systems; LLM-built graphs have no such guarantee.
agent_relevance: If the agent builds attack edges loosely, the accepted set can contain contradictory answers. Add a code check that accepted answers are mutually consistent.

source: Cramer and Guillaume (2019) Empirical study on human evaluation of complex argumentation frameworks (technical report)
finding: 61 participants judged arguments in 12 attack graphs (3 to 8 arguments) with natural-language text. Grounded and CF2 semantics were the best predictors of human choices. Grounded fits a simple strategy; CF2 fits a more demanding strategy used by some.
numbers: Prediction correct: grounded 74.97%, CF2 75.46%, preferred 68.42%, stage2 68.36%, semi-stable 62.84%, stage 62.79%. Chance 33%, all p<.001. Grounded vs CF2 p=.212. 86.7% of responses coherent; 49 of 61 participants coherent.
limits: Student sample, fictional scenario, 12 graphs only; stable excluded because it can give no extension.
agent_relevance: Humans mostly follow the simple grounded rule. Grounded is a defensible default for an S7 rule that people can audit.

source: Cramer and van der Torre (2019) SCF2: a semantics for rational human judgments on argument acceptability
finding: Combines normative principles and the empirical results to propose SCF2 semantics that fits what humans treat as rational. Frames the choice of semantics as open.
numbers: Builds on the Cramer and Guillaume data (a05). Only abstract and intro skimmed.
limits: Technical report; the new semantics is tested on the same small data.
agent_relevance: Semantics choice depends on the task; pick by what the agent needs, not by tradition.

source: Rahwan, Madakkatel, Bonnefon, Awan, Abdallah (2010) Behavioral experiments for assessing the abstract argumentation semantics of reinstatement
finding: First behavioural test of Dung semantics: people were shown attack chains where A attacks B attacks C and asked about belief in C. Reinstatement was only partly followed by people.
numbers: Exact N and percentages not read this session.
limits: Not opened; recorded from memory. Treat as unverified. DOI unchecked.
agent_relevance: Humans do not apply reinstatement perfectly; code will be more exact than people.

source: Polberg and Hunter (2018) Empirical evaluation of abstract argumentation: supporting the need for bipolar and probabilistic approaches
finding: Experiments with people suggest attack-only graphs miss support relations and uncertainty; bipolar and probabilistic extensions fit better.
numbers: Numbers not read this session.
limits: Not opened; from memory. DOI unchecked.
agent_relevance: Motivates the gradual and bipolar graphs (QBAF) the LLM work below uses.

source: Lagniez, Lonca, Mailly, Rossit (2021) Design and results of ICCMA 2021
finding: Reasoning in abstract argumentation is intractable in general, yet competition solvers handle it fast in practice. 9 solvers took part (7 exact, 2 approximate). The benchmark kept 165 instances from ICCMA 2019 and added 422 new ones.
numbers: Exact track covers complete, preferred, stable, semi-stable, stage, ideal semantics. Only two solvers were fully correct in a subtrack (global correctness issue noted).
quote: The most classical reasoning tasks in this kind of formalism are intractable in the general case
limits: Benchmark graphs are large synthetic ones, far bigger than candidate sets in an agent.
agent_relevance: Candidate graphs for S7 are tiny. Any semantics is instant. The cost is generating the edges, not solving.

source: Freedman, Dejl, Gorur, Yin, Rago, Toni (2025) Argumentative LLMs for explainable and contestable claim verification
finding: ArgLLMs ask an LLM for one supporting and one attacking argument per claim (depth 1) or recursively (depth 2, seven arguments), score each, and compute the claim strength with DF-QuAD in code. Accuracy is comparable to chain-of-thought, not higher.
numbers: Datasets TruthfulClaim, StrategyClaim, MedClaim; models Mistral, Mixtral, Gemma 7B, Gemma 2 9B, Llama 3 8B, GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4o mini, GPT-4o on MedClaim. 0.5 Base Arg variants were often 0.03 to 0.10 below CoT; Est. Base Arg D=1 mostly within about 0.03 of CoT. Depth 2 did not help over depth 1. Pilot on 2 validation sets of 200 samples. Table row labels garbled in extraction, so no single cell is quoted.
limits: Claims rewritten by LLMs then hand checked; one run per cell. Authors say models have limited zero-shot ability to generate and score arguments.
agent_relevance: Core evidence for S7-by-graph: an attack graph decided in code does not beat plain CoT on accuracy. Its gain is traceability and contestability.

source: Freedman et al. (2025) ArgLLMs: contestability properties
finding: Defines base-score contestability and argument-relation contestability for gradual semantics and proves DF-QuAD satisfies both: changing a base score or adding an attacker or supporter moves the claim strength in the expected direction only.
numbers: Proposition 1, proof in supplement. Quadratic energy semantics also reported in supplement.
limits: Property proved for DF-QuAD only; depends on LLM scores being meaningful.
agent_relevance: A code-computed answer can be audited and edited by a human by changing one edge. Useful for the multiplayer idea in memory.

source: Li, Fang, Chen, Li, Liao (2025) Enhancing conflict resolution in language models via abstract argumentation
finding: Zero-shot LLMs are poor at computing even the grounded extension of a Dung graph. Fine-tuning on 60,000 generated graphs with step-by-step explanations lifts accuracy to about 0.95 to 0.97. Explanations are what make it generalise.
numbers: AFs of 6 to 25 arguments, 60,000 samples. Grounded-extension accuracy zero-shot: Llama3-8B 0.18, GPT-3.5 0.15, Llama3-70B 0.37, Qwen2.5-7B 0.31, Qwen2.5-72B 0.48, GPT-4o 0.54. After SFT: Qwen2.5-SFT 0.97, Llama3-SFT 0.95. Models trained without explanations fell to about 30% on larger graphs (over 25 arguments).
limits: Synthetic graphs; trained models only on this task; robustness to noisy derivations tested only on grounded.
agent_relevance: Strong reason to compute the extension in code and never ask the LLM: the best frontier model got the grounded extension right only 54%.

source: Li et al. (2025) conflict resolution: ablation and conflict-resolution scores
finding: Training with the full logical explanation beats training with only results or masked parts. Conflict-free scores rise from 0.71 (Qwen) and 0.51 (Llama) before training to 1.00 after, under complete semantics.
numbers: CFP before training: Qwen2.5 0.71 (com) and 0.78 (prf); Llama3 0.51 and 0.45. ALSE before: Qwen 0.62 and 0.63; Llama 0.42 and 0.48. After SFT CFP 1.00; ALSE 0.99 (com), 0.95 or 0.86 (prf).
limits: Same dataset; GNN baselines are about as accurate on preferred.
agent_relevance: The model can be taught the procedure, but a few lines of code already do it exactly.

source: Zhu, Potyka, Hernandez, He, Ding, Xiong, Zhou, Kharlamov, Staab (2025) ArgRAG
finding: Build a QBAF from retrieved documents (claim-evidence and evidence-evidence edges annotated by LLM) and compute the verdict deterministically. It is the only RAG method that beats the no-retrieval baseline everywhere.
numbers: PubHealth, GPT-4.1-mini: no retriever 0.838, IC-RALM top10 0.670, CoT top10 0.647, ArgRAG top10 0.898. RAGuard GPT-3.5: no retriever 0.768, ArgRAG 0.804. GPT-4o-mini PubHealth 0.840 vs ArgRAG 0.855. Full graph beat claim-evidence only, mainly on RAGuard. Neutral base scores beat retriever scores. Euler, QE and DF-QuAD gave only minor differences.
limits: Temperature 0, one run; GPT models only; three paraphrased prompts for ablation. Gain over no-retrieval is small (0.01 to 0.06).
agent_relevance: Argument graphs help most when inputs conflict (noisy retrieval). Matches S7 with many conflicting candidates. Semantics choice is minor.

source: Zhou, Dejl, Freedman, Chen, Rago, Toni (2025) Evaluating uncertainty quantification methods in argumentative LLMs
finding: Plugging different UQ methods into ArgLLM argument scoring: plain direct prompting (ask for a confidence) is best or tied-best most often, beating more complex methods.
numbers: Bootstrap 5000 resamples, 180 pairwise confidence intervals. Direct prompting up to 0.130 higher accuracy than the next best (StrategyClaim, Gemma-2, 0.5 BS, D=1); its worst loss was 0.028 to LUQ. LUQ was strictly best 10 times; Semantic Entropy and Eccentricity once each.
limits: Each experiment run once; small models; scores binned into 20 quantile bins.
agent_relevance: Cheap self-reported confidence is enough for edge or node weights; do not pay for sampling-based uncertainty.

source: Ng, Jiang, Freedman, Rago, Toni (2025) MArgE: meshing argumentative evidence from multiple LLMs
finding: Merge argument trees from three small LLMs and let semantics decide. It beats single LLMs, ArgLLM ensembles and multi-LLM debate with a GPT judge.
numbers: Beats the best debate setup by up to 8.4%, at most 2.6% worse in the two cases debate won; MArgE-D1 beat all debate setups in 6 of 9 settings. With a stronger GPT-4o mini scorer: up to about 20% gains; beats its CoT by 3.5% and 1.0% on two of three datasets, loses on MedClaim. Also scoring the root claim adds +13.31% (+-1.83). Debate was sensitive to speaker order. Mean of 3 runs.
limits: Three datasets; med domain needs knowledge the small models lack.
agent_relevance: Code-decided merge of several attempts beats judge-decided debate. Agrees with G5 and G9.

source: Gorur, Rago, Toni (2024) Can LLMs perform relation-based argument mining?
finding: Building the edges is the weak link. Primed general LLMs classify support versus attack between argument pairs better than the RoBERTa baseline, but attack is harder than support.
numbers: Ten datasets, five open LLMs. Llama 70B-4bit macro F1 75 (best, 1.73 s per pair); Mixtral 8x7B-4bit 73 (0.28 s); Mistral 7B 70; baseline RoBERTa about 68 (table layout garbled). Mixtral attack F1 3 points below Llama 70B.
limits: Binary task only (no 'no relation' class); authors list ternary as future work.
agent_relevance: Edge quality is the bottleneck: roughly a quarter of pair labels are wrong. Test attack edges by running code where possible.

source: ART: Adaptive Reasoning Trees for explainable claim verification (2026)
finding: Replaces ArgLLM's isolated node scoring with pairwise tournaments between opposing arguments (Bradley-Terry strengths) then DF-QuAD. Outperforms ArgLLM in most cases and is on par with CoT; on larger models CoT is often better.
numbers: Intrinsic-strength setting gives about 3% relative accuracy gain over without. Multi-tree ensemble beats single trees; more tree breadth helps. ArgLLM is the special case with calibration parameter 0.
limits: Authors note extra branches add noise on large models. Author names not captured.
agent_relevance: Compare candidates pairwise rather than scoring each alone; matches S7 'run the one input where two rules differ'.

source: Nguyen, Nguyen, Cao (2026) Adaptive collaboration of arena-based argumentative LLMs (ACAL) for legal reasoning
finding: Multi-agent roles build an arena QBAF; clashes are adjudicated and low-confidence cases escalated. Small, mixed gains over CoT, RAG and multi-agent debate on LegalBench.
numbers: Gemini-2.5-Flash-Lite, Learned Hands Courts: ACAL acc 70.8, F1 70.7 vs CoT 69.3 and RAG 70.3; Hearsay acc 74.5 (ties MAD). Gemini-2.5-Flash Learned Hands: ACAL 75.5 acc, ties MAD 75.5, RAG 75.0, CoT 72.3.
limits: Differences of 0.5 to 1.5 points on single runs, no confidence intervals; two tasks only.
agent_relevance: Argument graphs are at best equal to strong baselines on accuracy; do not expect a boost from the graph itself.

source: Freedman, Dejl, Gould, et al. (2026) Neurosymbolic learning for inference-time argumentation (ITA)
finding: Training the argument generator and base-score model against the argumentation outcome (true/false/uncertain verdict) makes the graph route competitive with direct prediction. Untrained argumentative baselines were near 0.59 accuracy on TFU.
numbers: Qwen3-8B. TFU accuracy: untrained argumentative baselines about 0.59; best trained combinations about 0.668 to 0.677; direct SFT about 0.659 (read from a scrambled table, direction only). Base-score ranking agreement (Spearman) about 0.525 for untuned Qwen scores vs 0.944 for the best trained scorer.
limits: Table text extracted with scrambled rows; the row-to-number mapping is partly inferred.
agent_relevance: Raw LLM base scores are weak (rank agreement near 0.5); scoring needs a check or a better method.

source: Retrieval- and argumentation-enhanced multi-agent LLMs for judgmental forecasting (2025)
finding: Several argumentative agents (ArgLLM, relation-mining agent) with retrieval, merged into one framework, improve binary forecasting questions on Metaculus and GJOpen.
numbers: Metaculus: accuracy rises from 68% to 81% with retrieval and estimated base score. GJOpen: 63% to 75% in the best variant; less consistent; Guardian helped more than NYTimes. Gains were smaller where the agent was already strong.
limits: Gains vary by agent and source; combination does not always help.
agent_relevance: Support for merging several argument sources into one graph, with limits.

source: ArgRE: formal argumentation for conflict resolution in multi-agent requirements negotiation (2026)
finding: Uses the grounded extension over an attack graph among agent proposals; each accepted item is explained as defended against all attackers. Semantic preservation stays near baseline.
numbers: BERTScore F1 94.9%; compliance coverage 84.7%; trace completeness 40.9%; fast path under 30 ms for 95% of cases.
limits: Applied systems paper; proxy metrics; author list not captured.
agent_relevance: Grounded extension as arbiter of competing agent outputs is used in an applied system.

source: Argumentative reasoning with language models on non-factorized case bases (2025)
finding: Seen in an arXiv search listing as applying argumentation to case-based reasoning with LLMs. Not read.
numbers: Not read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Candidate for batch B.

source: Dung (1995), grounded extension as least fixed point
finding: The grounded extension is the least fixed point of the characteristic function F(S) = arguments defended by S; iterate F from the empty set. Every stable extension is preferred; every preferred is complete. Not opened; consistent with the tutorial definitions (a02).
numbers: Iteration ends in at most |A| steps on a finite graph.
limits: From memory; the tutorial confirms definitions, not the iteration theorem.
agent_relevance: The S7 computation is a short loop: unattacked candidates in, whatever they defeat out, repeat.

source: Dunne and Wooldridge; Dvorak and Dunne: complexity of abstract argumentation (surveys)
finding: Grounded extension is computable in polynomial time. Credulous acceptance under preferred is NP-complete; sceptical preferred is Pi-2-p-complete. Not opened; the ICCMA report (a08) confirms the general intractability.
numbers: Complexity classes from memory.
limits: Not read this session; DOI unchecked.
agent_relevance: Pick grounded for S7: the cheap case in the worst case.

source: Prakken (2010) An abstract framework for argumentation with structured arguments
finding: Original ASPIC+ paper. Not read; the 2013 tutorial (a02, a03, a04) is the source used.
numbers: None read.
limits: Not opened.
agent_relevance: Use the tutorial.

source: Amgoud and Ben-Naim (2017); Rago et al. (2016) DF-QuAD; Potyka (2018) quadratic energy: gradual semantics
finding: Gradual semantics give each argument a number from base score plus supporters and attackers. The LLM papers above use DF-QuAD and quadratic energy and report only small differences between them (a13). Not opened separately.
numbers: See a13 and a09.
limits: Secondary mention only.
agent_relevance: Use gradual semantics only if edges carry weights; unweighted attacks give grounded.
